transcript.reader:
Let me check I have the main claim before we start.

You're saying that computational complexity theory — resource bounds like the polynomial/exponential gap, not just "is it computable?" — hands philosophers new and useful tools for a list of specific problems: induction, the Turing Test and strong AI, logical omniscience, the semantics of computation, and so on. Is that a fair version?

Two questions.

1. Name one change to the world that would make you say philosophers should *not* care about complexity — some fact that could come out otherwise and that your case would treat as counting against it. If nothing on any list could do that, where does the thesis get caught out?

2. In section 3.3 you say a number counts as a "known" integer when we have an algorithm that writes its digits in time polynomial in their number of digits. Give me a near neighbour that would do the job just as well — "a proof I can check in polynomial time," or "a finite-step algorithm that provably terminates." If either works as well, what is it that actually holds "polynomial" in place?
transcript.author:
Your summary is fair, with one hedge I insist on: I claim complexity contributes useful perspectives, not that it dissolves these problems.

**1.** The load-bearing commitment is my identification of polynomial time with "feasible in practice." If that identification were systematically false — if growth rates simply didn't track tractability for bounded, real-world problems — Sections 3, 4, and 7 would lose their force, and I flag this in Section 12 as needing analysis. Second, a practical P = NP algorithm would gut Section 3: verification would collapse into finding, Hilbert's dream would effectively prevail, and my reason for thinking Penrose's speculation (*) unprovable *and* implausible would weaken. Third, if human cognition turned out to require exponential resources too, the asymmetry I use in 4.3 would evaporate.

But here I must concede something about the thesis's shape. It is a claim about relevance and illumination, not a prediction, so no single fact refutes "philosophers should care." The falsifiable part is small; the rest is a demonstration that a certain vocabulary clarifies certain puzzles. If that strikes you as too weak a target, you're right, and that's its honest status.

**2.** "A finite-step algorithm that provably terminates" will *not* do the job. p′ has that: I say in the text that we can write a program guaranteed to output p′, with an a priori bound on its steps. So that criterion fails to draw the line I want — which is exactly why the criterion must be complexity-theoretic.

"Checkable in polynomial time" is a genuine near neighbor, arguably closer to mathematical practice, since a proof *is* a checkable certificate. Under it, p is known via a Pratt/ECPP certificate. Whether p′ counts depends on certificates of primality and of no intervening prime — and whether we can produce those is itself a hardness question. So the criteria can diverge, which is a real cost of my stipulation.

What holds "polynomial" in place is stipulation: feasibly verifiable by a *known* algorithm, scaling with output size. I call it "the clearest basis I can suggest," not a theorem. Note Cramér's conjecture would promote p′ — the criterion is contingent on our algorithms.

transcript.reader:
Good — that's helpful, especially the concession that the "polynomial = feasible" step is a stipulation and the thesis is really an illumination claim.

Two more, each about one part and one change.

3. Section 4.1. Your lookup table shows the conversation-response function is computable, so "no fundamental obstacle to passing the Turing Test lives in computability theory." Swap the lookup table for any other merely *finite* thing — a finite automaton, a rigged dictionary keyed to the transcript. Does the argument still do its job? If it does, the part doing the work isn't "lookup table" but "the conversation is finite." So: what change to the world — an unbounded conversation, or agents with no fixed bit-bound — would make the argument stop working, and does anything in your case depend on that bound being 10^20 rather than any other number?

4. Section 6. You offer the claim that any chess-program-with-a-waterfall-oracle is matched by one without it, and you call it a *conjecture*, and flag that it hangs on a "reasonable" encoding. Two things. (a) Is that conjecture doing any work that the reduction lesson of 6.1 — "the reducing class must be weaker than the class reduced to" — doesn't already do by itself? (b) Name one change that would tell "the waterfall is really computing chess" apart from "it isn't." If no change on your list can, are those two the same claim at that level?
transcript.author:
**3.** Yes — you've put your finger on exactly the right joint. The lookup table's job is only to exhibit *a* finite, computable realization of f_B; a finite automaton or a rigged transcript-keyed dictionary would serve identically. The work is done by "the conversation is finite," not by "lookup table." I said as much parenthetically: the function is "indeed... recognized by a finite automaton."

What would stop it: if the conversation were unbounded — an idealization where agents converse indefinitely — then no finite table exists, and f_B could fail to be computable. *Then* computability theory could matter again. So my argument depends on the bound existing, not on its value. 10^20 is arbitrary; I chose it "to be generous" and gestured at the cosmological bound of ~10^122 bits. No part of the case depends on the specific number. That is why footnote 23 shifts to the asymptotic question — polynomial vs. exponential scaling of the resources needed to pass an n-length test — once finiteness alone won't carry the weight. The constant is a placeholder; the finiteness is load-bearing.

**4(a).** The conjecture is the content; 6.1 is only scaffolding. The reduction lesson tells you what *non-vacuous* equivalence must look like — reducing class weaker than class reduced to — but it doesn't by itself tell you that chess is not reducible to waterfall dynamics. That's the substantive empirical-mathematical claim, and I flag it as unproven. Concede: 6.1 alone can't deliver the anti-semantic conclusion.

**(b).** The change: an efficient, encoding-independent reduction from chess to waterfall-simulation, one that reads off good moves without itself solving chess. If waterfall dynamics were complete for chess that way, the encoding wouldn't be doing the work, and I'd have to say the waterfall really computes. Absent any such reduction — and absent exploitable physics structure — "the waterfall computes chess" and "some permutation exists" come apart only by the encoding, which is trivial for any bijection. At that level, I concede they are the same claim. The distinction is specifiable, but only by the reduction's existence — which remains conjectural.

transcript.reader:
Both concessions noted — the lookup table reduces to "the conversation is finite," and the waterfall claim bottoms out in a conjectural reduction.

Two more.

5. Section 7. Your job here is to answer "what do we mean by *simpler*," and to rescue the green/grue distinction. Poke it: name one change to the world that your PAC-plus-complexity story says would make a grue-ish hypothesis the *right* one, and one it says it would not — something we could actually look at. And: is "shortest program / most PAC-learnable" doing new work, or is it Occam's razor wearing a complexity costume? What would tell those two apart?

6. Section 5. The "infinity cure" turns "knows that P" into "can efficiently answer the infinite family around P." You then list three objections, and the third is that 8×8 chess is a *constant*, hence polynomial, so by the axioms a competent agent should already play it perfectly. Does the cure survive that objection, or does it show the whole account only works in an idealized limit and says nothing about the finite agents it was meant to explain? Name the change that would settle it.
transcript.author:
**5.** A change that would make a grue-ish hypothesis correct: if the world contained a genuine time-indexed law — emeralds really do shift color on a date, as Goodman's own example has them — then "grue" would be the short description and green the disjunction, and my story would endorse grue. It would *not*: a stationary world, where grue requires a disjunctive cut-off enumerating times. But I'll concede the sting: "shortest program" is short only relative to a fixed representation. Give me primitives under which grue is atomic and grue wins. So the answer to "what is simplicity" is partly stipulation, same weakness as the waterfall encoding.

Is it new work or Occam in costume? Conditional new work. PAC converts Occam folklore into theorems — Occam/Blumer-style bounds: a consistent hypothesis from a class of size |H| generalizes from ~log|H| samples. That's quantitative; folklore gives no sample count. But it can't justify the class or the encoding.

What tells them apart: a case where description length and learnability diverge — an uncomputable-but-short simplicity measure, or a class short to describe yet not PAC-learnable. Then "shortest program" and "most learnable" are distinct criteria, not one razor renamed.

**6.** Largely, no — it doesn't survive for finite agents. On the axioms, 8×8 chess is a constant, so polynomial, so a competent agent should already play it perfectly. That is absurd, and I admit it. My defense is the "usual response": asymptotic claims retain explanatory force until the constants prove ridiculous. But the honest reading is that the infinity cure is by construction a limiting case; Section 5.3 says complexity has "not yet come close" to solving omniscience for the finite agents we actually care about.

What would settle it: evidence whether resource thresholds for real bounded tasks track the polynomial/exponential line. If they routinely don't — exponential heuristics fine, polynomial algorithms useless in practice — the objector wins. Constructively, a complexity theory of genuinely resource-bounded finite agents, whose models are machines with fixed budgets rather than asymptotic families, would answer the objection directly instead of by appeal to the limit. That program doesn't exist yet.

transcript.reader:
Noted — grue bottoms out in the same representation-relativity as the waterfall encoding, and the infinity cure is, by your own account, a limiting case.

Two more.

7. Sections 10–11 (closed timelike curves, economics, equilibria). Your own ground rule (2) says a connection only counts if it draws on a *specific* complexity insight, not just "hard problems exist." Take the economics claim: finding equilibria is hard (PPAD-complete). What change would tell "complexity genuinely clarifies economic rationality" apart from "we found one more problem that happens to sit in a hard class"? Which single complexity result, if it had come out the easy way, would have killed your point — and which would have left it standing?

8. Scope. You fence off a large area ("What This Essay Won't Cover"): programming-language semantics, distributed systems, Kolmogorov complexity. Is that fencing a *held* limit — with a reason inside your argument for why those fall outside — or a *free* one that just says what you happened to ask about? Swap the fence for a neighbouring one (include Kolmogorov complexity); what breaks? And separately: you offer five reasons philosophers haven't engaged, then call the likely one a failure of communication. Name a change that would tell "philosophers haven't engaged enough" apart from "philosophers haven't engaged as much as I'd like."
transcript.author:
**7.** What tells it apart: not that equilibria are hard, but *why*. Nash existence is proven non-constructively via Brouwer; the class is PPAD — a total search problem, every instance guaranteed a solution, hardness arising from the existence proof itself rather than from a planted witness. That's the specific insight, and it's why the analogy to NP (witness-checkable) is misleading. If a polynomial-time algorithm for Nash had been found, my economic point dies: rational-actor models could then assume equilibria are computable, and "existence suffices" would be defensible. If Nash had merely turned out NP-hard, the cruder hardness claim survives but my specific claim — that guaranteed existence doesn't yield search, and that this is a distinct phenomenon from NP — would be undercut. So the easy-way outcome kills it; the wrong-hard outcome leaves the conclusion but guts the mechanism.

Concede: PPAD-completeness speaks to asymptotic instance families, not to any actual finite economy, and not to bounded human agents. Same limit-case caveat as Sections 5 and 3.3.

**8.** Mostly a *free* fence, and I should say so. Of the four excuses, only the "specific insight" ground rule does principled work — and it doesn't exclude Kolmogorov complexity; my Section 7 simplicity measure is essentially resource-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, which shows the fence already leaks. Including Kolmogorov complexity wouldn't break the essay; it would force two admissions: that "shortest program" and "most PAC-learnable" may be rival measures, and that plain Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable, so my Section 3.3 criterion needs the resource-bounded variant — which footnote 5 already concedes.

On the engagement gap: if the 32 philpapers, read closely, turned out competent and on-target, then my complaint is volume, i.e. preference, not deficit. If they turned out to misdescribe complexity — conflating it with computability, as I complain — that's a genuine, nameable failure. I'd need to survey them; I haven't.

transcript.reader:
Two more, then I think I have enough.

9. The hedge that runs through the whole essay — complexity "contributes useful perspectives," it doesn't "dissolve" problems. Poke it directly. What would we *measure* to see whether that hedge is swallowing real failures? In sections 5, 6, and 4.3 the answer keeps retreating to "still a perspective, in a limiting case." Is there any reading of the evidence that would make you say a given section offered *no* useful perspective at all? If not, what stops the hedge from being a catch-all with no gauge?

10. Section 4.2 — a polynomial-bounded Turing-Test-passer would be sentient, the exponential lookup-table one wouldn't. You say you're reluctant to take a position, and you call your point in 4.1 the "simpler, less controversial" one. Remove 4.2 entirely: which of your jobs stops getting done? If none does, is it an idle flourish, or is it load-bearing only for someone else's argument (Searle's critics) that you're reporting?
transcript.author:
**9.** Directly: the gauge is falsifiable content — does the section yield a *new distinction or question* we can state without the complexity vocabulary and test? If removing the section leaves the puzzle exactly as it was, no useful perspective was offered. By that gauge I'll name candidates: Section 6, if the waterfall conjecture is the content and it's unproven, may reduce to the 6.1 lesson about vacuous reductions — which Haugeland and Chalmers arguably already supply. report:
# Report: Aaronson, "Why Philosophers Should Care About Computational Complexity"

## 1. The question, frozen
The title makes one claim central: resource-bounded computation — not just "is it computable?" — gives philosophers something genuinely useful for the named puzzles (knowledge, AI, semantics, induction, quantum foundations, economics). Range: those problems. What is asked: a claim about *illumination*, not a cause and not a forecast — does the complexity lens yield a distinction you could state and check? The author agrees the falsifiable part is small, and lives in one place: "polynomial time = feasible in practice."

## 2. Jobs and parts
Jobs: (a) illuminate each named puzzle — **given**; (b) "polynomial tracks real feasibility" — the load-bearing job, which he admits is a **stipulation**; (c) each connection draws on a *specific* insight, not just "hard problems exist" (his ground rule 2) — **fixed**; (d) **added** by me: a section must yield a distinction statable *without* the complexity vocabulary. He accepted (d) as the gauge.

Parts, in the author's words: the feasibility identification; the "known integer" criterion; the lookup table and the finiteness bound; speculation (*); "polynomial → sentient"; the Cobham axioms and the "infinity cure"; the waterfall conjecture; PAC-simplicity and grue; PPAD-equilibria; new notions of proof; the scope fence; the "why philosophers haven't engaged" complaint.

## 3. Part by part
| Part | Mark |
|---|---|
| "Polynomial = feasible" (§3–4, §7) | **Held if** — held only by "growth rates track tractability everywhere that matters"; that job is in doubt for bounded, finite problems (his §12). |
| "Known integer" = poly-time write-out (§3.3) | **Fixed** — a stipulation ("clearest basis I can suggest"); a near neighbour, "poly-time checkable certificate," splits p from p′. |
| The lookup table (§4.1) | **Loose** — swap in a finite automaton; the job is done all the same. |
| The bound 10^20 bits (§4.1) | **Idle** — he says the value is arbitrary; remove it and nothing fails. |
| Finiteness of the conversation (§4.1) | **Held** — remove it (unbounded agents) and the argument stops; computability could matter again. |
| Speculation (*) (§4.1, §4.4) | **Held if** — held only by an unproven conjecture. |
| "Polynomial → sentient" (§4.2) | **Borrowed** — rests on Searle's critics; he reports it and declines to endorse it. |
| Cobham axioms / Theorem 1 (§5.1) | **Held** — a machine-free closure of "knowing how" that avoids omniscience; meets rule 2; he'd defend it hardest. |
| The "infinity cure" for real agents (§5.2–5.3) | **Held if** — held only by the job of explaining bounded knowers; 8×8 chess is a constant, so the cure says nothing about them, by his own admission. |
| The waterfall reduction (§6) | **Held if** — the content is a conjectural reduction resting on a "reasonable" encoding. |
| The 6.1 reduction lesson (§6.1) | **Borrowed** — a known fact about vacuous reductions; does not deliver the conclusion alone. |
| PAC → "what is simpler," grue (§7) | **Held if** — held by "description length = simplicity"; the separating case is unproduced. |
| PPAD / equilibria (§11) | **Held if** — the asymptotic insight is a theorem; its grip on any actual finite economy is doubtful. |
| New notions of proof (§9) | **Held** — interactive/zero-knowledge proofs are theorems that reframe "proof"; meets rule 2. |
| "Why philosophers haven't engaged" (§1) | **Unknown** — he hasn't read the 32 papers; reading them would settle it. |
| Closed timelike curves (§10) | **Unknown** — nothing tested here bears on it. |
| The scope fence ("won't cover") | **Loose** — he now calls it mostly free; it leaks (§7 already uses resource-bounded Kolmogorov complexity). |
| Ground rule 2 | **Held** — it does real work, by his own triage. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks
- **Flip.** It flips well at the level of results: a practical P = NP, a fast Nash algorithm, no PPAD hardness — he says each would kill a section. It does not flip at the level of the thesis: no fact refutes "philosophers should care," which he concedes.
- **Direction.** Mostly forward. §3.3 and §5 read a "known/able" status off the existence of algorithms — a backward reading (what we can tell) partly presented as what produces knowledge.
- **Answer in the starting points.** The job "a useful perspective" risks being the conclusion renamed. His counter — a new distinction testable without the vocabulary — is the right anti-circularity device, and he names sections (6, 4.3) that may fail it.
- **Pairs that pull.** (i) "Polynomial = feasible" vs "bounded real agents": strengthen the asymptotic identification and its grip on the finite agents philosophy cares about weakens. The line sits at "asymptotic has explanatory force until constants prove ridiculous"; he says thresholds routinely failing to track the line would move it. (ii) Reach vs falsifiability: each added section widens reach, but every retreat to "limiting case" loosens the whole.
- **Catch-alls.** The hedge "contributes useful perspectives" is a catch-all; he supplies a gauge only after being pressed, and never in the text.
- **Change list.** §4.2 is openly others' argument. The "won't cover" fence was presented as principled; he now calls it mostly free, and it leaks.
- **Rivals.** "Computability already gives these perspectives" (he argues complexity is *more* relevant); "plain Occam" against §7 (the separating case is untested).
- **Provenance.** §9, §11, §5.1 are **built** — theorems turned on a problem. §3.3, §7, and the applications are **fitted** to a stipulation or a track record. The thesis is **asserted/heuristic**. §4.2 and §6.1 are **borrowed**.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary
His own answer is the right one: pre-register, per section, a defeat condition — the observation that would show the lens adds nothing (e.g. for §11, bounded agents behaving as if equilibria were computed cheaply). That converts the hedge from a catch-all into a set of bets. Second: put the theorem/conjecture/reframing triage into the text, so a reader can mark the third category as decoration.

## 6. What this does not show
Passing is not truth. This measures whether each lens adds something checkable, not whether the philosophy is correct. Several parts are loose yet may be right.

## 7. One next step
For §5.1 — his hardest-defended section — write the defeat condition: the finite-agent observation that would show the Cobham axioms add nothing to the omniscience problem.
